Performance

How solar performs in clouds, winter and heat

Cloudy days, short winter days and hot summer afternoons each change what a system produces — and none of them mean solar is 'not working'.

Published 5 August 2026Updated 15 October 20266 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Every solar owner eventually has the same quiet worry: it clouded over for a week and the app's numbers fell. Or it was the middle of summer and mid-afternoon output looked unremarkable. Most of what looks like underperformance is simply weather and physics — but knowing the patterns is how you tell the difference between normal variation and a fault.

Clouds: output falls, but rarely to zero

Solar panels convert diffuse light as well as direct sunlight, so an overcast day still generates — just at a fraction of a clear day's output. Broken cloud is a mix of both: some moments near clear-sky performance between the clouds, some moments heavily reduced. A week of solid overcast in winter can feel alarming in the monitoring app and be entirely normal.

What matters for judging performance is the shape of the curve, not a single day: generation that returns to normal on the next clear day is weather. Generation that stays depressed through clear-sky weeks is worth investigating.

The temperature surprise

Panels are rated at a cell temperature of 25°C, and real-world cells run much hotter in full sun. The hotter they get, the slightly less efficient they become. This produces a counter-intuitive result: a crisp, clear autumn day at 20°C can deliver closer to rated output than a 40°C heatwave day, even though the summer sun is stronger. Heat also affects inverters, which derate their output when running hot — another reason ventilation around equipment is a design decision.

Winter versus summer in Australia

  • Southern states: winter days are shorter and the sun sits lower, so total daily generation falls well below summer levels — while heating loads push consumption up. The combination is why winter is when the grid does most of the work and batteries cycle hardest.
  • Cooler winter temperatures partially offset the shorter days; a clear winter midday can still produce strongly.
  • Northern Australia: the pattern inverts — the wet season's cloud cover, not the temperature, drives the seasonal swing, while the dry season delivers steady clear-sky generation.
  • Everywhere: the first winter after installation feels like a disappointment compared with the first summer. It is arithmetic, not failure — annual figures are what the system was sized for.

Reading your own system through the seasons

  1. Compare like with like: this March against last March, this bill against the same bill a year earlier.
  2. Judge clear days against clear days — pick a cloudless day in each season and compare curves.
  3. Expect the battery to fill less often in winter than in summer; state-of-charge graphs follow the seasons.
  4. Watch for step changes — a sudden, persistent drop on clear days is the signature of a fault, not weather.

Why estimates come as ranges

Weather is the largest single source of year-to-year variation in any solar estimate. That is why honest savings figures are presented as ranges with assumptions attached, and why a single poor week — or a single excellent one — should never be used to judge whether the system 'works'.

Design and habits that smooth the seasonal dip

  • Size the array around annual consumption, not summer generation — the annual figure is what pays back.
  • Shift winter-heavy loads (heating, hot water, laundry) into daylight where practical.
  • Review the electricity plan before winter, when usage patterns and prices squeeze hardest.
  • Keep December's numbers for comparison next December — a year of your own data beats any generic yield table.

Key takeaways

  • Overcast days reduce output but rarely eliminate it — solar runs on light, not just sun.
  • Hot days produce less per unit of sunlight than cool, clear ones; inverter heat matters too.
  • Winter shortens generation while raising consumption — the hardest season is expected to be hard.
  • Compare season to season, not week to week, and watch for step changes rather than dips.
  • Year-to-year weather variability is why savings estimates are ranges.
